21644-every-man-for-himself:
Hopkins Moorhouse opens Every Man for Himself in fog on Front Street, Toronto, in a tale copyrighted in Canada in 1920. A lone policeman writes in his patrol book under an arc light. A young athlete strides out of the gray vapour toward the docks.

Chapters turn on a tan satchel that keeps reappearing at key moments. A listening stenographer, a private car named Obaska, and trouble on the Winnipeg Express drive the plot. Kendrick makes a touchdown, McCorquodale explains, and a race begins. Moorhouse, who wrote Deep Furrows of the prairie west, here spins a brisk tale of money and mystery.
22526-cubs-of-the-wolf:
Cubs of the Wolf is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its characters argue about ridicule aimed at their own profession. Specialists, one complains, are the butt of enough ridicule already now.

Do something foolish, he warns, and the ridicule follows for life. Knees knock whenever anyone inquires about your specialty afterward. Worse, they threaten to read your thesis aloud in public. That academic dread gives the tale a wry, knowing start. Wolf cubs, by the title, suggest young predators or young trainees. Readers get a period story where status anxiety meets strange science. Its humor comes from experts fearing embarrassment more than danger.

Henrik Ibsen wrote this play in Christiania during 1894. Copenhagen published it on December 11 that year. William Archer translated it and supplied this introduction. Archer notes Ibsen's correspondence offers few clues to its origins.

One character, the Rat-Wife, has a definite suggested model. An old woman killed rats at Ibsen's childhood school. She carried a little dog in a bag, Ibsen told Prozor. Children were said to have drowned following her, like Hamelin's piper. Archer admits very little anecdotic history attaches to the play. richard-dare-s-venture-or-striking-out-f:
Edward Stratemeyer tells boys how Richard Dare struck out for himself, in a preface to the revised edition dated at Newark on March 1, 1899. The book is complete in itself, he says, yet opens his Bound to Succeed series. Readers and critics across the country had taken it warmly, to his surprise and thanks.

Richard is a country youth who finds nothing to do in his sleepy village and goes to New York to seek his fortune. He has almost no cash, but backbone and his mother's Christian teaching in plenty. City life proves no bed of roses, and snares meet him once he gains a footing. The New York street scenes, Stratemeyer adds, are taken from life.
the-complete-poems-of-sir-thomas-moore-c:
Sir Thomas Moore's complete poems, collected by himself with explanatory notes, open with a biographical sketch by William M. Rossetti. The sketch begins with the poet's birth in Dublin on the 28th of May, 1780, as the date is printed there.

His father was a grocer and spirit-retailer, called a spirit-grocer in Ireland. Thomas was schooled by Mr. Samuel Whyte, once Sheridan's first teacher, a man of more than average literary culture. Whyte encouraged acting among the boys, and Moore, bright and lively by nature, became a favorite and a leader in the school plays. His gift for verse showed early. In 1790 he wrote an epilogue for a piece acted at Lady Borrows's house in Dublin, and at fourteen he published a sonnet to Whyte in a Dublin magazine. Rossetti frames the poems with that rise from a tradesman's son to a national poet.
